question: A 34-year-old man presents with multiple painful ulcers on his penis. He says that the ulcers all appeared suddenly at the same time 3 days ago. He reports that he is sexually active with multiple partners and uses condoms inconsistently. He is afebrile and his vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals multiple small shallow ulcers with an erythematous base and without discharge. There is significant inguinal lymphadenopathy present. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent of this patient’s ulcers?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Multiple painful ulcers" -> "Sudden appearance" -> "Sexually active with multiple partners" -> "Inconsistent condom use" -> "Small shallow ulcers with erythematous base" -> "Significant inguinal lymphadenopathy" -> "Herpes simplex virus" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Multiple painful ulcers" -> "Sudden appearance" -> "Sexually active with multiple partners" -> "Inconsistent condom use" -> "Small shallow ulcers with erythematous base" -> "Significant inguinal lymphadenopathy" -> "Haemophilus ducreyi" -> 60%

CHAIN: "Multiple painful ulcers" -> "Sudden appearance" -> "Sexually active with multiple partners" -> "Inconsistent condom use" -> "Small shallow ulcers with erythematous base" -> "Significant inguinal lymphadenopathy" -> "Chlamydia trachomatis" -> 40%

CHAIN: "Multiple painful ulcers" -> "Sudden appearance" -> "Sexually active with multiple partners" -> "Inconsistent condom use" -> "Small shallow ulcers with erythematous base" -> "Significant inguinal lymphadenopathy" -> "Human papillomavirus" -> 30%
analysis: The presentation of multiple painful ulcers on the penis with an erythematous base and significant inguinal lymphadenopathy is most consistent with a herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection. HSV typically causes painful genital ulcers that appear suddenly and can be accompanied by lymphadenopathy. The other options are less likely: Human papillomavirus (HPV) usually causes warts, not ulcers; Chlamydia trachomatis can cause lymphogranuloma venereum, but the ulcers are typically painless; Treponema pallidum causes syphilis, which usually presents with a single painless chancre; Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid, which presents with painful ulcers but is less common and typically has a purulent base.
